items.title: Resolving the enforcement conundrum of emergency reliefs under Indian arbitration framework
items.summary: With the advancement of the institutional arbitration rules, interim measures as emergency relief in international arbitrations are an important tool to protect the rights of the parties pending determination of disputes. Therefore, the enforcement of an emergency order granted by emergency arbitrators is critical and holds significance for parties. This article examines the key issues in regard to the enforceability of emergency orders on the basis of seat under Indian legal regime and the legislative vacuum requiring change to make the Indian arbitration framework robust. Enforcement of emergency arbitrator order vis-a-vis arbitration seated in India The Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 (“Arbitration Act,1996) currently does not recognize an emergency arbitrator order. However, the Supreme Court in the case of Amazon NV v/s Future Retail recognized emergency arbitrator orders by holding that the interim order by emergency arbitrator in arbitration seated In Indian are enforceable in India in the same manner as an interim order granted by the arbitral tribunal under Section 17 of the Arbitration Act, 1996. Thus, emergency relief orders for arbitration seated in India are enforceable as a decree of court under Section 17(2) of the Arbitration Act, 1996. Enforcement of emergency arbitrator order vis-a-vis arbitration seated outside India Notable the Amazon NV judgement is limited to orders passed by the emergency arbitrator in an arbitration seated in India. Thus, as things stands today, there exists no direct route under the Indian legal regime to seek the enforcement of an order passed by the emergency arbitrators otherwise. In the absence of any provision for the recognition and enforcement of foreign interim orders, the only avenue available to parties, unless otherwise agreed, is to institute a petition under Section 9 of the Arbitration Act, 1996 seeking reliefs identical to those sought before the emergency arbitrator. State of West Bengal & Ors.]. Justice Partha Pratim Roy observed that making the requisite application and paying the fee to the local authorities for operating a temporary book stall is not enough without explicit permission for operating such a stall. "In view of the law laid down by the Hon’ble Division Bench in MAT 1881 of 2026, a person who approaches the Court will have to be first established whether the said party has a permission for erecting a stall or not. Therefore, the protection as sought for by the petitioner requires establishing, that they had a valid permission to run the bookstall. In the present case, such permission is absent. In view of the law declared by the Hon’ble Division Bench, the writ petitioner is not entitled to any relief as prayed for," the Court said. CPI(M) moved the Court after some people, allegedly belonging to the KMC and accompanied by a large police contingent and a bulldozer, attempted to remove the stall on October 17. Keeping up with the same practice, they applied for permission to set up the book stall to the office of Assistant Director SWM-I, Borough – X, Kolkata Municipal Corporation. A fee amounting to ₹3,208 was also paid to the concerned KMC department in this regard. A letter to that effect was also sent to the concerned officer-in-charge of the nearby police station . items.title: Andhra High Court sets aside earlier order directing SEC to consider voters’ lists
items.summary: Follow TNM ’ s WhatsApp channel for news updates and story links. A division bench of the Andhra Pradesh High Court on Monday, October 19, set aside an earlier order directing the State Election Commission (SEC) to issue clear orders to its officials to consider voters’ lists updated up to July 15, 2026. A division bench of Justices Mandava Kiranmayi and Alapathi Giridhar passed its order against the backdrop of local body polls in the state. Hearing the SEC’s appeal against the single bench order, the two judges ruled that the SEC could decide on the final electoral roll based on its own circulars. On October 16, the YSR Congress Party (YSRCP) had approached the High Court. YSRCP had alleged that the SEC had failed to consider its representation seeking publication of the final voters’ lists for local body elections. The representation sought publication after resolving claims and objections received up to August 31, 2026, regarding additions, deletions and corrections to the draft electoral rolls under the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. The party had sought directions to ensure the final electoral rolls reflected all approved changes before the elections were conducted. The single judge had directed the SEC to issue instructions to the concerned authorities to consider the voters’ lists updated up to July 15, 2026. Keep independent journalism alive. items.summary: The suicide of Chennai-based financial influencer V Harish on Tuesday, October 20, has triggered allegations of cyberbullying against another YouTuber, Jason Samuel, who is known for exposing alleged fraud by content creators. Harish, who operated the Instagram account ‘Finance With Harish’ and had over 1.3 million followers, died by suicide at his residence in Muttukadu, Chennai. He was a well-known figure in Tamil Nadu’s content creator community. A few days before his death, Harish’s Instagram account was suspended over allegations of illegal activity. Harish’s father, J Vinayagam, lodged a police complaint alleging that Jason had subjected his son to sustained cyberbullying, defamatory posts and threats, causing him severe mental distress. According to the complaint, Jason published videos and posts on October 18 accusing Harish of fraud and misleading the public. Jason, who has previously called out several content creators, including A2D, Parithabangal and PUBG Madan , had accused Harish of offering financial advice and asking his followers to invest money without being registered with the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI). Jason alleged that Harish’s activities were illegal and demanded he furnish proof of his registration. However, a video recorded before his death has surfaced in which Harish accused Jason of attempting to extort money from him. “If I have committed any wrongdoing, you can question it. And I will answer it, but my five years of hard work are being stolen,” Harish said in the video. He alleged that Jason had tried to extort money from him by claiming to have connections with several politicians in Puducherry and threatening to publish a series of videos against him if he did not pay. Harish also accused Jason of defaming him and subjecting him to mental harassment. Harish’s death has drawn condemnation from members of the content creator community, several of whom have alleged that he was driven to suicide by cyberbullying. Meanwhile, Jason denied cyberbullying Harish, saying that he had only questioned the influencer’s credentials and alleged violations of financial regulations. Jason claimed that Harish lacked the necessary SEBI registration to operate as an investment adviser and had misrepresented his credentials in relation to the Association of Mutual Funds in India (AMFI).
